{{Short description|Australian engineer and herpetologist (1923–1999)}}
'''Kenneth R. Slater''' (22 June 1923 - 15 August 1999)<ref name="EDR">Beolens, Bo; Watkins, Michael; Grayson, Michael (2011). ''The Eponym Dictionary of Reptiles''. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. xiii + 296 pp. {{ISBN|978-1-4214-0135-5}}. ("Slater, K.",  p. 245). Retrieved through [https://books.google.com/books?id=3ovZoFyLhzkC&dq=ken+slater+snake&pg=PA245 GoogleBooks], 18 June 2017.</ref> was an Australian [[Civil engineer|engineer]] and [[herpetologist]].<ref name="PM">Mirtschin P (2006). "The pioneers of venom production for Australian antivenoms". ''Toxicon'' '''48''': 899-918. (Slater is in pages 911 and 912). Retrieved [http://www.venomsupplies.com/assets/Pioneers-published-paper.pdf online], 18 June 2017.</ref> Slater's deliveries of [[snake venom]] were instrumental in the development of [[antivenom]] for several species.

==Biography==
Slater was educated as a civil engineer, but he was interested in [[zoology]] and [[snake]]s, as well. In his early years, he accompanied [[Eric Worrell]] a few times, searching for live snakes in the Australian wild.<ref>Markwell K in Cushing N. ''[http://medicalhistorymuseum.mdhs.unimelb.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0010/1942084/From-SnakeHandlers-to-wild-entrepreneurs.pdf From snake handlers to wildlife entrepreneurs] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190306061138/https://medicalhistorymuseum.mdhs.unimelb.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0010/1942084/From-SnakeHandlers-to-wild-entrepreneurs.pdf |date=2019-03-06 }}'', Medical History Museum Melbourne website. Retrieved 18 June 2017.</ref> In 1952, he took a job in the oil industry in [[Papua New Guinea]], to be able to spend more time in the wild.<ref name="PM" /> Shortly after, he was appointed acting animal ecologist by the Department of Agriculture of the PNG government. Just over a year after returning to Australia, Slater was appointed senior wildlife officer for [[South Australia]] in 1960, followed by a position as acting wildlife biologist for the [[Northern Territory Administration]] in 1963.<ref name="PM" /> He also worked some time for Worrell's [[Australian Reptile Park]], caring for, and milking, snakes for just under a year (1959-1960).<ref name="PM" />

===Snake venom===
Slater was an experienced snake collector and snake milker. In his Papua New Guinea years, he supplied the [[CSL Limited|Commonwealth Serum Laboratories]] (CSL) with their first samples of [[Coastal taipan|Papuan taipan]] venom.<ref name="PM" /> He also provided all the [[Papuan black snake]] venom CSL used to develop and produce an antivenom for the species. This antivenom turned out to be effective for [[snakebite|bites]] of the [[Mulga snake|king brown snake]], as well. In 1955, CSL provided Slater, Worrell, and [[Ram Chandra (snake showman)|Ram Chandra]] with some of the first doses of Taipan antivenom, in recognition of the dangers involved in their work.

==Taxonomy==
Slater described ''[[Oxyuranus scutellatus]] canni'', [[Common name|commonly]] known as the coastal or Papuan taipan, in 1956. He named it after George Cann, longtime [[Snake Man of La Perouse]].<ref>Slater K (1956). ''[http://www.kingsnake.com/aho/pdf/menu6/png/slater56.pdf "On the New Guinea taipan"]''. ''Memoirs of the National Museum of Victoria'' '''20''': 201-205. (''Oxyuranus scutellatus canni'', new subspecies). Copy at kingsnake.com, retrieved 25 June 2017.</ref>

Slater is commemorated in the scientific name of a species of Australian lizard, ''[[Slater's desert skink|Liopholis slateri]]''.<ref name="EDR"/>
